key: Like a son cherished in his father’s house, Let our oblation rise unto the Gods.
s: After the singer imagines trading places with Agni, the hymn returns to the offering; Sāyaṇa, on 8.19.27, takes the cherished son as Agni, fed with offerings like a son by his father, who carries the oblation to the gods from the house of sacrifice.

evidence.words: “पितुर्न “पुत्रः पितुः पुत्र इवास्माकं “सुभृतः सुष्ठु भर्ता । यद्वा । पित्रा पुत्र इवास्माभिः सम्यग्भृतो हविर्भिः पोषितः । अयमग्निः पुत्र इवास्माकं सुभृतः “दुरोणे यज्ञगृहे “देवान् “आ अभिलक्ष्य “नः अस्माकं "हविः “प्र “एतु प्र गमयतु ।
evidence.gloss: Like a son of a father, our good supporter; or else, like a son by a father, well maintained by us, nourished with oblations. This Agni, well maintained by us like a son, in the house, the house of sacrifice, towards the gods: let him send our oblation forth.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, 8.19.27 at [638,27]); packet Sanskrit pitur na putraḥ subhṛto duroṇa ā devāṁ etu pra ṇo haviḥ is the app’s 8.19.27. Sāyaṇa gives subhṛtaḥ two ways and settles on Agni well maintained by the worshippers with oblations as a son by a father, duroṇe as yajñagṛhe, and pra etu as pra gamayatu (let him send forth the oblation to the gods); Wilson’s “Cherished by us as a son by a father, let him (Agni) in our dwelling convey promptly our oblation to the gods” follows him. His alternative (yadvā: let Agni come, and the oblation reach the gods) is not the one named, and the sentence claims only the first. Plain sense faithful: 8.19.25 and 26 imagine Agni mortal and the singer immortal, and 8.19.27 turns to the oblation; no four-word run. Revision 402086 dated 2024-04-30 by the wiki API. Entry-check ok.
